article.title: Car Accident Claims
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. California’s comparative fault rules allow people injured in car accidents to seek compensation even when they share some responsibility for the crash, although their compensation may be reduced by their percentage of fault. Ventura, California, is a coastal city where drivers travel along busy roads, local streets, and major routes such as Highway 101. Traffic congestion, changing road conditions, and driver mistakes can contribute to collisions throughout the area. After a crash, consulting a Ventura, CA, car accident lawyer can help an injured person understand how fault may affect an insurance claim or personal injury lawsuit. California follows a pure comparative negligence system. Under this rule, an injured person can recover damages even if they are found to be mostly responsible for an accident. However, the amount awarded is reduced according to their share of fault. Understanding California’s Comparative Fault Rule Comparative fault is used when more than one person may have contributed to an accident. For example, one driver might have been speeding while another made an unsafe turn. Investigators, insurance companies, or a court may consider the actions of both drivers when determining responsibility. California’s system differs from rules in states that prevent people from recovering damages if their share of fault reaches a particular threshold. In California, a person may still recover compensation even if they are found 90% responsible, although the recovery would be reduced substantially. The legal foundation for this principle includes the California Supreme Court’s decision in Li v. Yellow Cab Co. (1975), which adopted comparative negligence in California. How Shared Fault Can Reduce Compensation The percentage of fault assigned to an injured person directly affects the damages they may recover. Consider a situation in which a driver suffers $100,000 in total damages but is found 20% responsible for the accident. If the remaining 80% of responsibility belongs to another party, the injured driver’s recoverable damages would generally be reduced to $80,000. The calculation is straightforward, but determining the correct percentage of fault can be more complicated. Each party may present different accounts of the collision, and the available evidence may support more than one interpretation. Insurance companies may argue that an injured driver was speeding, distracted, or failed to take reasonable steps to avoid a crash. The injured person may dispute that assessment based on witness accounts, photographs, vehicle damage, or other evidence . Evidence Can Help Establish Responsibility Evidence plays an important role in determining how an accident happened. Useful records may include: Police or collision reports. Photographs and videos of the scene and vehicle damage. Statements from eyewitnesses . Traffic camera or dashcam footage. Medical records documenting accident-related injuries. Expert analysis when the circumstances require it. Drivers should preserve relevant evidence and provide accurate information when reporting an accident. They should avoid guessing about details they cannot remember or making assumptions about fault before the facts are clear. How Insurance Companies Evaluate Fault Insurance adjusters review available information to assess liability and the value of a claim. They may consider traffic laws, driver statements, damage patterns, medical documentation, and other relevant records. An adjuster’s initial assessment is not necessarily the final determination of fault. If the parties disagree, additional evidence or legal proceedings may be needed to resolve the dispute. Before accepting a settlement, an injured person should understand what expenses and losses it covers. A settlement agreement may also limit the ability to seek additional compensation for the same accident later. Why Legal Guidance May Help Car accident claims can involve disputed facts, medical expenses, lost income, and disagreements about future losses. Legal guidance can help an injured person understand California’s comparative fault system, organize supporting evidence, and evaluate a settlement offer. A lawyer can also explain the possible effect of shared responsibility on a claim and identify deadlines that may apply. Under California Code of Civil Procedure Section 335.1, the general deadline for filing many personal injury lawsuits is two years from the date of injury, although exceptions may apply. Claims involving government entities can have much shorter deadlines. Key Takeaways California follows a pure comparative negligence system. An injured person can generally seek damages even if they share responsibility for a collision. Compensation is reduced according to the injured person’s percentage of fault. Police reports, photographs, witness statements, and medical records may help establish what happened. Legal deadlines and settlement terms should be reviewed carefully.
